https://newpol.org/a-reckless-drive-for-.text: A Reckless Drive for More Nuclear Power By: Stanley Heller September 4, 2026 [PDF] [Print] A structure damaged by a Russian strike in June 2026 near a site where Chernobyl spent fuel rods are stored Over the last year the energy and environmental agency of Connecticut’s government held four presentations to encourage more nuclear power plants in Connecticut. The first thing to say about them is that they start with the wrong assumption. They assume our biggest challenge is the need for more energy to power data centers so the economy can use more AI. Wrong. There is a critical problem, actually an extraordinary crisis, but it’s not the need for more energy. The crisis is the worsening climate catastrophe , a calamity arriving at lightning speed. Back in 2018 the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) gave a grim report that said we must cut back greenhouse gas emissions by nearly half by 2030 or face not only many more weather and fire devastations but the prospect of going over tipping points from which humankind could not recover. The massive fires in Europe are a small taste of the calamity we face. So we have only a few years to deal with an existential danger. That, and not AI, has to take front and center. We have to take emergency measures now. Data centers and AI development belong in the backseat. The good news is that mitigation of climate ruin is possible and it doesn’t require nuclear power. In fact, nuclear power is a dangerous diversion. At present there’s one nuclear plant running in Connecticut, by the name of Millstone. There had been a legal ban against more nuclear reactors in the state but that was overthrown by Governor Ned Lamont and the legislature in 2025 . The legislature then appropriated $5 million to find towns that say they are willing to be sites of nuclear power plants. The presentations from Connecticut’s Department of Energy and Environmental Protection (DEEP) are intended to warm the public to both varieties of nuclear generation, uranium-powered fission plants and deuterium-tritium fusion plants. Both have inherent defects. Fission One huge and obvious problem with fission is radioactive waste. In the nuclear power process radioactive uranium is mined, then enriched and formed into rods and the uranium goes through a process that splits its atoms and gives off energy. That’s done until the rods are no longer productive. Then they are classified as “spent”. However, spent rods are incredibly radioactive and intensely hot. So these rods are put in cooling ponds of the facility for at least five years. Then they have to be stored indefinitely. Nuclear power waste has been around for more than 80 years, but in all that time there has been no way found to dispose of it permanently. There was a plan to put 90,000 tons of high-level radioactive waste deep under Yucca Mountain in Nevada, but state leadership and the residents were vehemently against it. Nevada’s official position is that the area is “seismically and volcanically active, porous and incapable of geologically containing the waste.” So, the high-level and long-lasting radioactive waste produced by the nation’s civil nuclear power plants remains at the 75 sites — both operating and closed – where they were created. The problem is managed by the advanced engineering process called “kick the can down the road.” How are they stored on site? After being removed from the fuel storage pools, the waste is put inside what are called “casks”, stainless steel containers welded shut surrounded my more steel or concrete. How long will a cask last without leaking? One speaker at the Connecticut forums, a professor of nuclear engineering named Dr. Sukesh Aghara , said the casks were good for 160 years while Mark W. Goodsbey , who is Director of Safety and Licensing at Millstone said, “Temporary storage is still designed for hundreds and thousands of years of service without any significant impact or concerns to their robustness.” Thousands of years? How can you assure us of that? Are the storage areas for spent fuel rods hardened against military attack? The answer is, “No”. To most of us the very question would seem ridiculous. Who would be stupidly reckless enough to attack a nuclear power plant? After the attack on the Chernobyl’s New Safe Containment on Valentine’s Day 2025 and the drone attack a few hundred yards from Chernobyl’s spent fuel casks in June 2026 , we know that any force ruthless or terrified enough may make such an assault. There is a concept called Hardened On-Site Storage . It would require the casks be stored in areas hardened against terrorist and armed force assault in facilities resembling hardened missile silos. Of course, that would cost a lot of money. When we see pictures of actual casks, they’re above ground in the open (to shed heat) one next to another. No U.S. plant is hardened to HOSS standards. The speakers at our public meetings here in Connecticut talk about small, advanced power plants that are modular, in that one day their parts could be built in a factory banged out one after another like pre-fab houses. They use the acronym “SMR” for them (small modular reactor). Paul Dickman of the National Academies of Science stated right out that the large plants (1,000 MW and more) are more efficient than the SMRs. So why build them? A claimed advantage of the SMRs is that they will only need small emergency planning zones around them to protect the public. The “current fleet” (their words) of reactors typically has 10-mile emergency planning zones around the plants. With the new SMR’s professor Aghara said “you’re talking about less than 5 miles, ideally about two miles.” At another point Kati Austgen of the Nuclear Energy Institute said the zone could be “a 400 meter diameter area.” She said a plant might be able to demonstrate to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission such safety measures that the zone would be ending right at the site boundary “meaning there would be no need to pre-plan any sort of evacuation in the area surrounding the plant.” No emergency planning zone? So they want to build these things right in the middle of cities, anywhere, maybe even next to schools and hospitals. The ancient Greeks called this insolent arrogance “hubris.” We haven’t talked about cost. Professor Aghara says he thinks there will be a “30 to 40% reduction in the cost of energy when you couple nuclear and renewable and storage.” However, a 2024 report from the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis states, “A key tenet for SMR proponents is that the new reactors will be economically competitive. But the on-the-ground experience with the initial SMRs that have been built or that are currently under construction shows that this simply is not true. There currently are three operating SMRs worldwide—two in Russia and one in China, plus a fourth under construction in Argentina. Costs for all four have been significantly higher than originally forecast.” SMR boosters say assembly line construction of SMRs will save lots of money, but these assembly lines don’t exist anywhere. At this stage it’s just a theory and with global warming putting us in immediate peril we don’t have time to test it out. Past experience with large nuclear plants is not encouraging. Connecticut residents know all about it. The owner of Connecticut’s Millstone plant, Dominion Energy, threatened to shut it down because the nuclear plant couldn’t compete with natural gas. Not until the legislature cut it a deal were the threats tabled. One big, supposed advantage for the plants is that they’re super-reliable. We’re told they function 24/7. But it’s not true. For one thing they have to be taken offline for refueling and maintenance. The U.S. Energy Information Administration says that averages 34 days a year. And we’re realizing now the plants depend on the weather. When it gets too hot outside they have problems. Nuclear plants rely on drawing cool water from rivers or the sea to remove heat from reactor systems. But witness France this year . Nuclear power plants there had to shut down already three times this summer. Hot release water combined with exceptionally warm river water would have killed aquatic life. What’s turning out to be a bigger problem is that in heat waves river water levels drop so the water sometimes can’t be drawn upon for use in the plants. Witness Hungary in August 2026. It had to shut down its nuclear reactors due to low water levels for the first time in its history. Its pumps couldn’t get water at so low a level. Romania shut down its nuclear plant, too. And the final problem is time. Remember there are only three SMRs anywhere in the world. The idea that SMRs could be produced quickly is untested. Nuclear power plants have been taking 17 years on average to plan, build and get online so SMRs are not going to be of any help in a climate crisis that’s imminent. Fusion The U.S. started releasing huge amounts of energy from fusion in 1952. That was the year of first hydrogen bomb explosion. Of course, that energy couldn’t be channeled into anything but mass destruction, but the science was correct. With enormous heat and pressure, you could set off a fusion reaction. In the H-bomb enormous heat came from an atomic bomb “trigger”. Ever since scientists and engineers have been working on how to do fusion on a much smaller scale and in a controlled way. Magnets, lasers and other means are being tested as ways to confine incredibly hot elements in their plasma state during fusion reactions. There’s never been a fusion power plant. Only in 2022 did the National Ignition Facility arguably produce more energy from a fusion experiment than the amount used by the lasers to conduct the experiment, a net gain of roughly one megajoule of energy or 0.3 of a single kilowatt hour. Even that is kind of fake. It didn’t take into account the 400 megajoules of electricity needed to power the lasers! But there are tens of billions of dollars floating around for nuclear experiments and construction, so companies are being formed willy nilly to gather in those dollars. Why not? It’s very challenging physics and materials engineering, rewarding work which is presumably well paid. Three companies presented at the DEEP forum. They claim they’ll be producing electricity from fusion in the early 2030s. But wait. There are as they say “challenges”. I’m relying mostly on an article by Daniel Jassby called “Fusion reactors: Not what they’re cracked up to be.” It was in The Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists in 2017. Dr. Jassby has serious credentials. He was a principal research physicist at the Princeton Plasma Physics Lab until 1999. For 25 years he worked in areas of plasma physics and neutron production related to fusion energy research and development. Jassby says there are “four regrettable problems with nuclear energy: radiation damage to structures; radioactive waste; the need for biological shielding; and the potential for the production of weapons-grade plutonium 239.” What? Did you read that last one right, the process can create weapons-grade plutonium? One of the draws of fusion was that it was so safe. Fusion just used sweet simple hydrogen isotopes for fuel. Alas, as Jassby puts it, “A fusion reactor can become a source of weapons-grade plutonium simply by placing natural or depleted uranium inside the reactor vessel, where the high neutron flux will produce plutonium 239.” Fusion of hydrogen produces helium, huge amounts of energy and lots and lots of neutrons. Stick uranium into the reactor and you can produce plutonium which you can make into a nuclear weapon. Shouldn’t that disqualify fusion right from the git go? Should humanity be building these plants everywhere, giving tyrants and unstable governments the materials to build nuclear bombs? Let’s briefly talk about one other problem mentioned by Jassby. As Jassby explains, fuel assemblies themselves will be transformed into tons of radioactive waste to be removed annually from each reactor as would lots of other parts of the machinery. In fact, he says, “While the radioactivity level per kilogram of waste would be much smaller than for fission-reactor wastes, the volume and mass of wastes would be many times larger .” So what’s the gain with fusion? Finally, the time problem for fission goes double, triple or more for fusion. Companies may talk about fusion giving out power in the 2030s but no one knows if it really can be done. There’s been a fusion project in the south of France called ITER, sponsored by a number of countries including the U.S. and Russia that. It was thought up in 1985. Building started in 2010. National Geographic had a lengthy article about it in its November 2025 issue. The ITER first “energy-positive” fusion isn’t expected until 2039 (See page 43). And that energy will be heat not electricity. We Don’t Need Nuclear We already have the solution, a way of avoiding going over the climate cliff. It’s a combination of solar, wind, water, batteries, efficiency and mandatory conservation. Stanford University civil and environmental engineering professor Mark Z. Jacobson has been explaining for nearly 20 years that we can power the U.S. without burning fossil fuels or splitting or fusing the atom. He demonstrates it in detail state by state and for the entire country . Part of the solution is efficiency. The energy with the least waste is the energy not used in the first place. We need a crash program in everything from insulation to triple-hung windows. Since America’s leaders on the whole ignored the dire warning of climate scientists and we only have a few years before tipping points are crossed, we have to add to Jacobson’s ideas. We need to plan a strict conservation system in which we use fossil fuel for what’s absolutely necessary and sharply cut back on the rest. Data centers and AI should be put on hold. Personal jets should be grounded. When facing catastrophe you deal with it. You don’t do business as usual. I’m not much good about predictions but I’m going to say these expensive dangerous plants will not be built in CT. However, a lot of time and effort will be needed to stop them. It’s time we don’t have. I mentioned the year 1952 earlier in the article as the date the first hydrogen bomb exploded. 1952 was also the year of the Paley Commission, a project of the Truman administration, which saw the promise of solar and recommended its wide use. Linda Pentz Gunter of the group Beyond Nuclear has written the “Paley Commission’s authors recognized the abundance offered by solar energy, observing in 1952 that, ‘the United States supply of solar energy is about 1,500 times the present requirement.’” The Commission called for “aggressive research in the whole field of solar energy.” Unfortunately, the report was ignored. Eisenhower became president in 1953 and he launched “Atoms for Peace” driving the U.S. down the disastrous path of nuclear power. We don’t have the time for another reckless diversion. This is precisely how women who fled Ukraine for EU countries at the start of the war described their experiences of living under temporary protection to Suspilne. This summer, the European Union and Switzerland extended temporary protection for Ukrainians already living there until 4 March 2028. For new arrivals, however, the rules have changed: applicants must now prove that they have been exempted from military service in Ukraine and left the country legally. Meanwhile, for many Ukrainians who have been living in the EU for several years, temporary protection means ever-deeper integration into the lives of the countries that have taken them in. According to Eurostat, there are currently over 4.4 million Ukrainians living in the EU who were previously granted temporary protection. With every month of the war, the number of those returning to Ukraine is decreasing, believes Ella Libanova, director of the Institute of Demography and Social Studies at the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine. At the same time, in her view, it is most likely that women aged over 25 with a higher education will return. After all, back home they have significantly better prospects for professional development. Suspilne spoke to Ukrainian women who were granted temporary protection in Poland, Germany and Ireland during the early years of Russiaâs full-scale invasion. It also sought to find out the views of men who have moved to the EU and hold this status. Poland: Ukrainians are needed, but attitudes are deteriorating Inna Bezroda has been living in Poland since 2022: she moved there from Kyiv with her two children after the full-scale war began. Inna has cancer, so her husband joined her a year later after leaving Ukraine legally. Because of her illness, Inna is unable to work, so her husband provides for the family. The family rents a flat in Warsaw. Apart from child benefit, to which working parents are entitled in Poland, the family receives no other social benefits. Thanks to her husbandâs job, Inna is entitled to health insurance and free cancer treatment. Inna Bezroda, a Ukrainian woman, left for Poland in 2022 when the full-scale Russian invasion began | photo from a personal archive, courtesy of Suspilne If she were living in Poland on her own, she would have lost her right to access healthcare from March 2026 onwards â due to new changes to the law. These changes have deprived those who are not in work of free access to medical care. Vulnerable groups â pensioners and people with disabilities â are the hardest hit by this. The Temporary Protection Mechanism in the EU was introduced specifically for Ukrainian refugees on 4 March 2022 in response to Russian aggression. It grants the right to reside and work legally in the EU. Ukrainians are granted this status without lengthy bureaucratic procedures. As part of this scheme, in addition to the legalisation of their status, they were granted access to state healthcare and assistance with renting accommodation. However, year after year, individual countries review various aspects of the temporary protection arrangements for Ukrainians within the framework set by the European Union. This applies both to access to healthcare and to the provision of accommodation. Furthermore, such protection will come to an end once the EU recognises that it is safe to return to Ukraine. At the same time, Ukrainians are sometimes helped by charitable organisations or individuals outside this formal framework. âI lived in Warsaw for three years in a flat with my children for free; it was given to us by a Polish man, a complete stranger,â says Inna. âI recently went on a rehabilitation programme for cancer patients, where I was the only Ukrainian. I was worried about how people would treat me. But everything went brilliantly; I made friends with the Polish women. We talked about politics, and I admitted to them that Iâd been afraid to come v and I felt a lot of support. They said: "If you ever hear that we Poles have a negative attitude towards Ukrainians, just think of our faces.â However, Inna acknowledges that attitudes towards Ukrainians in Polish society as a whole have deteriorated compared with 2022. Although her command of Polish is limited, Inna avoids speaking Ukrainian on public transport so as not to cause offence. "We used to joke about it in the family: if Poland comes up with anything else [regarding Ukrainians], weâll get in the car, pack our bags and head further west." Poland is home to over 970,000 Ukrainians under the temporary protection scheme, the second-highest figure in the EU after Germany. Most of them (68 per cent, according to the UN Refugee Agency) are in work, as the country provides virtually no social support. Many Ukrainians are in jobs below their qualifications, whilst a significant number are still working remotely for Ukrainian employers or running their own businesses. Ukrainiansâ contribution to Polandâs budget exceeds the cost of supporting them: in 2024, the countryâs GDP grew by 2.7 per cent thanks to refugees. Warsaw therefore has a financial interest in keeping Ukrainians in the country â despite the anti-Ukrainian rhetoric of politicians. According to Inna, her family isnât particularly concerned about how long the EUâs temporary protection programme will last. After all, Poland has already introduced a scheme allowing Ukrainians to switch to a different, more permanent status known as CUKR. This new status is not dependent on having a job or a certain level of income, which is particularly important to Inna. Ukrainians who held temporary protection status in Poland as of June 4, 2025, and whose status remains valid at the time of application may apply for the Temporary Residence Permit (TRP). TPR status will be temporary (three years â Ed.), but the time spent under this status will count toward the period required to obtain long-term EU resident status. Inna and her family are planning to apply for the new status in the autumn, once it becomes clear how the new system works in practice. âWe meet the criteria, so weâre planning to apply for this status,â she says. âWeâll see what happens next: weâre taking each day as it comes and arenât making too many plans for the future.â The family has no plans to return to Ukraine: despite missing home, Inna fears she will not be able to receive the treatment she needs there. She has not yet personally noticed any deterioration in attitudes towards Ukrainians in Poland. Germany: an uncertain future for the unemployed and men Further west, in Germany, the situation for Ukrainians is significantly different. As of May 2026, 1.3 million Ukrainian refugees there had been granted temporary protection status â the so-called Paragraph 24. Recently, there has been an increase in the number of men among them. According to the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees, 60 per cent of Ukrainians who have entered Germany since March 2025 are men of conscription age. Overall, in the EU, one in four Ukrainians with temporary protection is a man aged between 18 and 64. Maksym, a Ukrainian (name changed at his request), is living in Berlin under temporary protection from the EU. When Russiaâs full-scale invasion began, he was abroad, so he decided not to return to Ukraine. In Germany, Maksym continues to develop his own tourism business, which is linked to Ukraine and caters to Ukrainian clients. Ukrainians in Dresden | Imago / Scanpix âFor four years, Iâve been living as someone who is waiting for the war to end â so that we can live a normal life, because my business depends on it,â he says. âThe fate of my 17 or 18 employees and our company depends very much on Ukraine. And we havenât changed this strategy, because we believe the war will end and weâll return to some sort of normal life.â Maksym is critical of the restrictions imposed on Ukrainian men â both those introduced by Ukraine and those approved by the European Union in July 2026. "It was thought that if we didnât close the borders, everyone would leave Ukraine. But I, for one, would rather come here than leave," he says. "My main problem is that I canât move about freely. I canât come to Ukraine and go about my business." However, Maksym doubts that the European Unionâs decision not to accept newly arrived men from Ukraine will deter those who wish to leave. âIt will more likely mean that those fleeing Ukraine will find protection outside the EU â in Albania or Turkey,â he believes. Suspilne also tried to obtain comments from other Ukrainian men who had left for the EU during the war. We asked at least 13 men and sought comments in refugee groups on social media â all of them refused to speak to us. The proportion of Ukrainians with temporary protection in Germany who are in work is relatively low â 39 per cent. This is one of the lowest figures in the EU. The reasons for this are not limited to access to social benefits, which are generous in Germany. They also include the specific nature of the local labour market, which is rather closed, and the countryâs approach to the integration of foreigners, who must first learn the language and either validate their qualifications or acquire new ones. Oksana Mediana, from Kyiv, used to work as a manager at a fitness club in Ukraine. She has been living in Hamburg with her two children and her mother since 2022, but has not yet managed to find a job there. âAll these years Iâve been learning the language and attending integration courses. Iâve reached B2 level in German and am trying to get my qualifications recognised. Iâm trying to find a job as an assistant and am willing to do any office work â but itâs proving difficult,â she says. Oksana lives in a small rented flat, the rent for which is partly subsidised by the state, and receives social security benefits. Oksana Mediana, from Kyiv, has been living in Hamburg with her two children and her mother since 2022, but has not yet managed to find a job there | photo from a personal archive, courtesy of Suspilne Once the temporary protection programme comes to an end, Ukrainians like Oksana will have few options for remaining abroad legally. Germany allows Ukrainians who have a permanent employment contract, are studying at university or are married to a local citizen to switch to other types of residence permits. âAs long as I donât have a job, I have no options. You canât switch to a different status if youâre not self-sufficient,â says Mediana. Oksana Medianaâs husband has been serving in the Ukrainian Armed Forces since 2022 and occasionally comes to Germany to visit his family. Oksana wants to return to Ukraine, but admits that for her children, aged 9 and 13, Germany has become a second home. She says that over time, her ties with her homeland have weakened: her father has died, and many of her relatives have also moved abroad. âIâm still in limbo. I hope the war will be over tomorrow, that my husband will ring and tell me to come home,â says Oksana. âThe children donât really want to go back anymore. Weâve been to Ukraine a few times, but we donât have a large family there anymore.â Ireland: permission to stay depends on employment and accommodation Nataliia Minailo arrived in Ireland with her one-year-old daughter in the spring of 2022. At first, she had hoped to return home within a few months, but when a Russian missile struck her house in Vyshhorod, near Kyiv, killing a neighbour, she decided to stay in Dublin for longer. When her daughter started nursery, Natalia began studying at college to become a tour guide, as she had a degree in history from Ukraine. âI knew right from the start that temporary protection wouldnât last forever. So, when I finished college, I started looking for a job. Even though people told me: Just stay on benefits, then you can come back to Ukraine. Iâve been working since October 2024,â says Nataliia. She currently works part-time at a museum and also runs her own private guided tours of Dublin. Nataliia Minailo, a Ukrainian woman, arrived in Ireland with her one-year-old daughter in the spring of 2022. She works part-time at a museum and also runs her own private tours of Dublin | photo from a personal archive, courtesy of Suspilne 120,000 Ukrainians have been granted temporary protection in Ireland â this is the eighth highest figure in the EU, although in reality around 84,000 still live there. The rest have returned home or moved to other countries. In May this year, the country introduced the option for Ukrainians to switch to a different type of residence permit, which ultimately leads to permanent resident status. To qualify, you must have lived in Ireland under temporary protection status for one year and meet strict criteria regarding employment and accommodation: you must have been in employment or self-employed for the past six months, earn at least â¬29,432 per year, and live in private accommodation without receiving any housing benefit from the state. Applications for this new status will be accepted from September 2026. However, the housing crisis in Ireland makes the transition to a new status a difficult task for Ukrainians. As of the end of 2025, 68,400 Ukrainian refugees in Ireland (82 per cent) were living in state-provided accommodation or accommodation paid for by the state. There is a severe shortage of commercial housing in the country: to rent a property, you need to have a job and an income several times higher than the rent, as well as beat dozens of other applicants. For most Ukrainians, this is practically impossible. Dublin is one of the most expensive European capitals, where renting a two-bedroom flat costs an average of 2,241 euros a month. Nataliia, like many Ukrainian refugees, is still living with an Irish family: many Irish people opened their homes to Ukrainians in 2022. However, the government has announced that it is phasing out payments to those who take in Ukrainian refugees. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA/AP Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex Met refers itself to police watchdog over Meghan warning letter Move comes as Philippines police investigate suspected child sexual abuse images reportedly found at Thomas Markle Sr’s former home PA Media Thu 29 Oct 2026 13.36 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Metropolitan police say they have voluntarily referred themselves to the official watchdog for failing to pass on a letter detailing allegations against the Duchess of Sussex’s father. The announcement comes as police in the Philippines investigate suspected child sexual abuse images reportedly found at Thomas Markle Sr’s former home. Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, told the Sun last week that he found a stash of child sexual abuse images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines and reported it to local police and the FBI. Markle Sr has admitted paying for sex in the south-east Asian country but denies possessing illicit material. The Met said it received a letter in 2019 in which the author suggested “they were writing to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex”. The Met said although the letter “did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom”. It was passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, the force said. It added that – after a review – a voluntary referral had been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct “in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex”. Commander Adam Slonecki, who leads the Met’s protection command, said: “In January 2019, the Met received a letter addressed to our protection command, specifically the fixated threats assessment centre. “The author of the letter suggested they were writing to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex. While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. “The letter was assessed and subsequently passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. “The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies. In recent days, the Met’s directorate of professional standards has carried out an initial review into our actions following receipt of the letter in 2019. “Following that review, a voluntary referral has been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. “In addition, it is our intention to make a number of referrals to relevant overseas law enforcement agencies in relation to the allegations contained within the letter. That process is under way and will be completed in the coming days.” Explore more on these topics Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex Metropolitan police Police Philippines Monarchy London news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/ue/d.text: Pe măsură ce negocierile privind încetarea focului se intensifică, unii lideri europeni și-au exprimat dorința ca un negociator supererou să îi înfrunte pe Vladimir Putin și Donald Trump, să obțină un acord de pace echitabil pentru Ucraina și să asigure securitatea continentului, notează Politico . Aceasta era deja opinia diplomaților și a oficialilor apropiați de discuții, cărora li s-a acordat anonimatul pentru a se putea exprima cu privire la procesul sensibil de pace din Ucraina, care divizează opiniile în capitalele europene, chiar înainte ca UE să decidă vineri că acesta va trebui să fie un efort colectiv. Dorința de a desemna un singur reprezentant care să vorbească în numele Europei era de înțeles. Atractivitatea ideii de a avea un singur lider respectat care să preia frâiele se bazează în mare măsură pe dorința de a proiecta puterea și unitatea europeană — precum și pe interesul de a asigura eficiența și eficacitatea negocierilor cu Rusia, SUA și Ucraina. Președintele Ucrainei, Volodimir Zelenski, a declarat chiar el săptămâna aceasta că dorește ca Europa să stabilească în câteva zile cine îi va lua locul la negocieri și a sugerat că ar prefera să fie vorba de o singură persoană (a indicat chiar că are o preferință, deși nu a dezvăluit niciun nume). Nu a reușit să-și atingă scopul. În schimb, liderii prezenți vineri la summitul de la Dublin au decis că grupul E5 , format din patru mari țări ale UE — Germania, Franța, Polonia și Italia — și Regatul Unit, alături de reprezentanți ai Comisiei Europene și ai Consiliului, vor continua lucrările în echipă. Căutarea unui reprezentant de vârf care să ocupe locul Europei la masa negocierilor în cadrul următoarei runde de discuții de pace devenise o obsesie politică la Bruxelles, care a trecut cu vederea cel puțin două aspecte importante. În primul rând, negocierile nu se desfășoară în prezent la nivel de conducere. Discuțiile din această săptămână de la Abu Dhabi au fost discuții tehnice între înalți funcționari. Marile personalități politice, precum Putin și Zelenski, nu au fost prezente, ca să nu mai vorbim de Trump. Rusia a trimis un consilier al Kremlinului să conducă echipa sa, iar Ucraina l-a însărcinat pe șeful serviciilor sale de informații să prezinte punctul de vedere al țării. Dacă acești oficiali vor înregistra progrese în vederea încheierii unui acord, liderii vor dori, fără îndoială, să se implice. În cele din urmă, liderii vor fi cei care vor semna orice acorduri de pace care vor urma — și nu există nicio limită în ceea ce privește numărul de președinți sau prim-miniștri din UE care ar putea participa la o astfel de reuniune în calitate de semnatari sau garanți ai acordului final. Următorul pas necesar, potrivit atât Ucrainei, cât și reprezentanților SUA care mediază negocierile, este ca Europa să se alăture discuțiilor cu Rusia — la acest nivel tehnic. Al doilea aspect pe care unele state membre și persoanele din cercurile de la Bruxelles nu l-au luat în considerare este de natură structurală: există pur și simplu prea mulți actori europeni cu interese și competențe la fel de importante, dar foarte distincte, ceea ce face imposibilă consolidarea tuturor acestor aspecte sub autoritatea unei singure persoane. Comisia nu poate negocia viitoarea arhitectură de securitate a Europei — această decizie revine membrilor NATO și capitalelor naționale. Dar, la rândul lor, nici NATO, nici Parisul, nici Berlinul nu pot negocia sancțiunile UE sau aderarea Ucrainei la Uniune — aceste aspecte țin de competența Comisiei. Iar ideea că E3 — marile puteri economice și militare ale Europei, adică Germania, Franța și Regatul Unit — ar lăsa Comisia, Consiliul European sau NATO să se ocupe de toate acestea în numele lor nu este realistă. După cum a afirmat un diplomat al UE: „Motivul pentru care Europa nu a găsit o singură persoană care să o reprezinte în ansamblu este că Europa nu este un superstat”. În contextul negocierilor privind Ucraina, interesele europene includ numeroase state membre ale UE, dar și țări precum Regatul Unit și Norvegia, precum și Turcia și Republica Moldova, a afirmat diplomatul. „Cine poate promite trupe pe teren în numele restului Europei? Cine poate oferi finanțare în valoare de miliarde? Este dificil”. Concluzia la care au ajuns unii oficiali implicați în procesul de la Abu Dhabi a fost că Europa ar trebui să fie reprezentată de o echipă, așa cum s-a întâmplat deja, deși până acum aceasta s-a aflat la un pas distanță de sala principală de negocieri. Diferiți membri ai acestei echipe se vor ocupa de diferite aspecte. Apoi se pune problema conținutului: ce se va discuta și care va fi poziția colectivă a echipei Europei? „Ceea ce spunem de fapt este mai important decât configurația exactă a participanților din sală”, a declarat prim-ministrul Suediei, Ulf Kristersson, în timp ce se îndrepta către reuniunea liderilor UE de vineri. Motivul pentru care oficialii americani și ucraineni doresc participarea Europei este că aceștia consideră că inițierea unei discuții privind reorganizarea structurilor de securitate ale continentului ar putea determina Rusia să adopte o abordare mai cooperantă. Vladimir Medinski, principalul negociator al Rusiei, a declarat că principalul subiect discutat săptămâna aceasta la Abu Dhabi a fost cadrul de securitate al Europei: „Conflictul din Ucraina a demonstrat că întregul sistem de securitate instituit după conferințele de la Ialta și Potsdam funcționează defectuos, iar în Ucraina a explodat un abces”, a afirmat el. Delegația Ucrainei a remarcat că poziția intransigentă a Rusiei s-a mai atenuat puțin atunci când reprezentanții Moscovei au văzut ocazia de a discuta despre pretențiile lor mai ample privind securitatea europeană. Însă Europa însăși nu a făcut parte din acea discuție. Primul aspect care trebuie clarificat se referă la ordinea etapelor negocierilor — și, mai ales, când ar trebui europenii să se hotărască să discute cererea Rusiei de a reforma securitatea regională? Aceasta este o întrebare crucială și, potențial, existențială pentru țările europene. Și este deja un subiect asupra căruia înalții oficiali ai UE își evaluează cu atenție pozițiile. Persoanele apropiate discuțiilor consideră că se poate găsi o modalitate ingenioasă de a propune Rusiei un dialog privind securitatea regională, ca parte a unei planificări atente a etapelor negocierilor, fără a integra complet această chestiune în acordul final de pace pentru Ucraina. Însă diferiți purtători de cuvânt ai UE fac declarații contradictorii cu privire la această chestiune legată de ordinea de desfășurare, ceea ce poate fi interpretat fie ca o strategie inteligentă, fie ca un semn al haosului continuu. Kaja Kallas, cea mai înaltă reprezentantă a diplomației UE, a declarat că nu trebuie să se discute despre o arhitectură de securitate europeană mai amplă — cum ar fi configurațiile NATO, desfășurările de trupe și forumurile de lucru pentru consultări cu Rusia — până la finalizarea acordului de pace. Însă la Abu Dhabi, oficialii UE și-au exprimat disponibilitatea de a permite desfășurarea în paralel a unor linii de negociere, astfel încât soluția de pace pentru Ucraina și viitoarele structuri de securitate ale Europei să poată fi discutate în același timp. De asemenea, oficialii din capitalele naționale sunt de acord că ordinea negocierilor pe această temă este esențială. În culise, diferite țări și facțiuni au opinii diferite cu privire la strategia potrivită, în timp ce se confruntă cu dilema dacă este sau nu corect să se angajeze direct într-un dialog cu Putin. Și, desigur, problema rolului Europei ar putea fi încă irelevantă. Reprezentanții SUA au declarat joi seara că Putin a fost de acord ca Europa să se alăture negocierilor, dar Kremlinul a pus la îndoială acest lucru vineri. După încheierea negocierilor de la Abu Dhabi din această săptămână, Jared Kushner, ginerele lui Trump și trimis special, a recunoscut cele două probleme cu care se confruntă. „Dacă Europa ar putea desemna o singură persoană care să vorbească în numele ei, aceasta ar fi o realizare mai mare decât încercarea de a-i convinge pe ruși să o includă în negocieri”, a afirmat el. Ce urmărește cu adevărat Rusia în negocierile cu Ucraina.
